lessonData.subject: Science / Biology
lessonData.tagline: How a single cell clones its genetic blueprint to grow, heal, and sustain life.
lessonData.overview: Mitosis is a vital type of cell division where one parent cell divides to form two genetically identical daughter cells with the exact same chromosome number. By replicating DNA before division and precisely separating sister chromatids, multicellular organisms can grow, heal wounds, and replace worn-out tissues throughout life.

diagram.title: Stages of Mitotic Division
diagram.description: The sequential process of DNA duplication, alignment, chromatid separation, and cell cleavage.

nodes.label: DNA Replication (Interphase)
nodes.details: Before division begins, each chromosome makes an identical copy of its DNA, forming twin sister chromatids joined at a centromere.

nodes.label: Equatorial Alignment (Metaphase)
nodes.details: Chromosomes condense tightly and line up individually along the center of the cell, attached to spindle fibers.

nodes.label: Chromatid Separation (Anaphase)
nodes.details: Centromeres split, and spindle fibers pull identical sister chromatids apart toward opposite poles as individual chromosomes.

nodes.label: Two Identical Daughter Cells
nodes.details: Nuclear membranes reform around each set of chromosomes, and the cell cleaves into two genetically identical daughter cells.

chalkNotes.title: Cell Division by Mitosis
chalkNotes.subtitle: Nuclear Division Conserving Chromosome Number
chalkNotes.coreRuleOrFormula: Parent Cell (2n) → DNA Duplication → Sister Chromatid Separation → 2 Identical Daughter Cells (2n each)
bulletPoints: DNA replication occurs before mitosis: each chromosome forms two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere.
During mitosis, chromosomes align at the spindle equator, sister chromatids separate to opposite poles, and new nuclei form.
Chromosome number is conserved (e.g., diploid remains diploid); mitosis never halves chromosome counts.
Mitosis serves four core functions: growth from a zygote, tissue repair, cell replacement, and asexual reproduction.
keyTakeaways: Mitosis produces exactly 2 genetically identical clone cells with no loss of chromosomes.
Mitosis never stops in adulthood; it continuously regenerates skin, blood, and healing tissues.

quiz.question: A horse skin cell has a diploid number of 64 chromosomes (2n = 64). If this cell divides by mitosis to repair an injury, how many daughter cells will form, and how many chromosomes will each daughter cell contain?
quiz.explanation: In mitosis, a single parent cell divides once to yield exactly 2 daughter cells. Because chromosomes replicate their DNA before dividing, the full diploid chromosome number is conserved: each daughter cell receives the exact full complement of 64 chromosomes. Halving to 32 chromosomes occurs only during meiosis to produce gametes.

suggestedQuestions: Which organelle in an animal cell carries genetic instructions inside chromosomes?
If an adult organism has stopped growing taller, why does mitosis still occur billions of times every day?
What would happen to the chromosome count in future generations if sperm and egg cells were made by mitosis instead of meiosis?

cell-division-by-mitosis.title: Stages of Mitotic Cell Division
cell-division-by-mitosis.description: How a single cell duplicates and divides its genetic material to produce two identical cells.

nodes.label: DNA Duplication
nodes.details: The cell grows and creates an exact replica of all its DNA before division begins.

nodes.label: Chromosome Alignment
nodes.details: Copied chromosomes condense and line up straight across the center of the cell.

nodes.label: Chromatid Separation
nodes.details: Spindle fibers pull identical sister chromatids apart toward opposite ends of the cell.

nodes.label: Two Daughter Cells
nodes.details: The cytoplasm divides, forming two genetically identical cells essential for growth and repair.

key-properties-of-cell-division-by-mitos.title: Key Properties of Mitosis
key-properties-of-cell-division-by-mitos.description: This diagram illustrates how a parent cell divides once to create two genetically identical cells for growth and tissue repair.

nodes.label: Parent Cell
nodes.details: A single body cell duplicates its DNA so that both upcoming cells will receive a complete set of genetic instructions.

nodes.label: Single Nuclear Division
nodes.details: Duplicated chromosomes align in the center and separate equally during a single round of nuclear and cell division.

nodes.label: Two Identical Daughter Cells
nodes.details: Results in exactly two daughter cells with the same number and kind of chromosomes as the parent cell.

nodes.label: Growth and Tissue Repair
nodes.details: Provides new identical cells that allow an organism to grow larger and replace damaged or worn-out tissues.

real-world-applications-of-cell-division.title: Real-World Applications of Mitosis
real-world-applications-of-cell-division.description: Explores how mitotic cell division enables growth, wound healing, and asexual reproduction in living organisms.

nodes.label: Mitotic Cell Division
nodes.details: A mother cell divides to form two identical daughter cells, providing exact genetic copies needed across the body.

nodes.label: Growth and Development
nodes.details: Allows a microscopic fertilized egg to grow into a trillions-of-cells human, and saplings to grow into tall trees.

nodes.label: Wound Healing and Regeneration
nodes.details: Generates new skin and bone cells to close wounds, mend fractures, and replace worn-out red blood cells daily.

nodes.label: Asexual Reproduction & Plant Cuttings
nodes.details: Used by organisms like Hydra for budding and farmers to grow whole new fruit trees from simple branch cuttings.

main.title: The Process of Mitosis
main.why: It shows that DNA replicates before the cell splits, visually proving why each daughter cell retains the full original chromosome count.
main.checkQuestion: If the parent cell started with 64 chromosomes, how many chromosomes end up in each daughter cell based on this diagram?

steps.name: Start with parent cell
steps.caption: We begin with a single parent cell containing its original chromosomes.

steps.name: Show DNA replication
steps.caption: Before dividing, the cell makes an exact copy of its DNA, forming X-shaped chromosomes.

steps.name: Show cell division
steps.caption: The cell splits, sending one copy of each chromosome into each new daughter cell.

contrast:mitosis-halves-chromosomes.title: Does Mitosis Halve Chromosomes?
contrast:mitosis-halves-chromosomes.why: This visualizes how DNA replication happens before division, showing that every daughter cell receives a full, identical set of chromosomes.
contrast:mitosis-halves-chromosomes.checkQuestion: Looking at the two paths, why is copying the DNA first essential for the daughter cells?

steps.name: Show the halving rule
steps.caption: If we just split 46 in two, we get 23 chromosomes each.

steps.name: Show replication phase
steps.caption: Wait, what if the DNA copies itself to 92 before splitting?

steps.name: Show identical cells
steps.caption: Now, 92 chromosomes split into two cells of 46.

steps.name: Compare results
steps.caption: Compare the two outcomes; which one keeps the cell's identity?

contrast:mitosis-halves-chromosomes.focus: Mitosis halves the number of chromosomes because the cell divides into two.

contrast:mitosis-stops-in-adults.title: Does Mitosis Stop at Adulthood?
contrast:mitosis-stops-in-adults.why: This visualizes the constant necessity of mitosis in an adult body, contrasting the misconception of it stopping with the reality of cell turnover and repair.
contrast:mitosis-stops-in-adults.checkQuestion: If mitosis stopped at adulthood, how would your body react to a scratch or a scrape?

elements.text: X Rule: Mitosis stops at adulthood

steps.name: Anchor the rule
steps.caption: Let's look at the rule that mitosis stops when we become adults.

steps.name: Introduce the challenge
steps.caption: If this rule were true, what happens to skin cells that die or get damaged?

steps.name: Show the real process
steps.caption: In reality, the body must replace those cells to heal the area.

steps.name: Check understanding
steps.caption: Looking at this, why must mitosis continue even in an adult body?

contrast:mitosis-stops-in-adults.focus: Mitosis stops occurring once an individual reaches adult size.

contrast:mitosis-produces-gametes.title: Mitosis vs. Meiosis
contrast:mitosis-produces-gametes.why: Visualizing chromosome count demonstrates why mitosis, unlike meiosis, cannot be used to produce gametes without doubling the chromosome number every generation.
contrast:mitosis-produces-gametes.checkQuestion: Looking at the result of mitosis, what would happen to the chromosome count in the next generation if these daughter cells fused?

elements.text: What happens to the chromosome number if we use mitosis to make gametes?

steps.name: Show the starting parent cell
steps.caption: Both processes start with a parent cell containing 4 chromosomes (2n=4).

steps.name: Model the mitosis path
steps.caption: If a cell divides by mitosis, it creates a clone with the same number of chromosomes.

steps.name: Model the meiosis path
steps.caption: Meiosis divides the chromosome number in half to create gametes (n=2).

steps.name: Prompt reflection
steps.caption: Compare the resulting cells; why does the body require meiosis for reproduction?

contrast:mitosis-produces-gametes.focus: Mitosis produces sperm and egg cells.

visualsDeclined.3d: Mitosis is essentially a flat, sequential process of division best visualized as a 2D diagram rather than a 3D volume, as the complexity lies in the arrangement and segregation of chromosome pairs.
